content: Willows, belonging to the family of trees and shrubs, exhibit significant variation in size and growth habits. However, they share many common characteristics. There are approximately 350 species of willows globally, predominantly found in moist soils within cooler regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Willows are highly cross-fertile, resulting in numerous hybrids, both naturally occurring and cultivated. Some smaller species are also referred to by the common names osier and sallow, the latter derived from the Latin word salix. Certain arctic and alpine willow species are notably small, such as the Dwarf Willow (Salix herbacea), which rarely grows taller than 6 cm but spreads extensively across the ground. The Weeping Willow, widely planted as an ornamental tree, is a cultivar (Salix × sepulcralis 'Chrysocoma') derived from a hybrid between the Chinese Peking Willow and the European White Willow. Description Willows are characterized by their abundant watery sap, furrowed and scaly bark rich in salicylic acid, soft yet tough and pliant wood, slender branches, and large, fibrous, often stoloniferous roots. These roots are particularly notable for their resilience, size, and vitality. The leaves of willows are deciduous, typically elongated but occasionally rounded or oval in some species, with serrated edges. All buds are lateral, as willows do not form terminal buds. These buds are covered by a single scale, which encloses two minute opposite buds at its base. The leaves are alternate, except for the first pair, which fall off when they reach about an inch in length. Willow leaves are simple, feather-veined, and often linear-lanceolate in shape. They are usually serrated, rounded at the base, and acute or acuminate at the tip. Their coloration varies widely, ranging from yellow-green to blue-green. Flowers Willows are dioecious, meaning male and female flowers grow on separate plants. These flowers appear as catkins, which emerge early in the spring, often before the leaves or as the new leaves begin to open. The petioles of the leaves are short, and the stipules are often conspicuous, resembling small round leaves that may persist for half the summer. In some species, however, the stipules are small, inconspicuous, and short-lived. The staminate (male) flowers lack both calyx and corolla, consisting solely of stamens (ranging from two to ten) accompanied by a nectariferous gland. These are inserted at the base of a scale borne on the rachis of a drooping raceme, known as a catkin or ament. The scale is oval, entire, and densely hairy. The anthers are rose-colored in the bud but turn orange or purple upon blooming. They are two-celled, with the cells opening longitudinally. The filaments are threadlike, pale yellow, and often hairy. The pistillate (female) flowers also lack calyx and corolla, consisting of a single ovary accompanied by a small flat gland. The ovary is one-celled, with a two-lobed style and numerous ovules. The fruit is a one-celled, two-valved, cylindrical, beaked capsule containing numerous minute seeds furnished with long, silky, white hairs that aid in wind dispersal. The catkins typically appear before or alongside the leaves. Cultivation Most willow species root easily from cuttings or broken branches that come into contact with the ground. Notable exceptions include the Goat Willow and Peachleaf Willow. A famous example of willow propagation from cuttings involves the poet Alexander Pope, who planted a twig from a parcel tied with twigs sent from Spain to Lady Suffolk. This twig thrived, and legend has it that all of England's Weeping Willows descended from this original tree. Willows are often planted along stream banks to stabilize the soil with their interlacing roots, which protect against water erosion. In many cases, the roots of willows are significantly larger than the stems that grow from them. Ecological Issues Willows serve as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species. In Australia, several willow species were historically planted for erosion control along watercourses. However, they are now considered invasive weeds, and many catchment management authorities are actively removing them to replace them with native trees. Uses Medicinal Uses The leaves and bark of the willow tree have been recognized for their medicinal properties since ancient times. Texts from Assyria, Sumer, and Egypt mention their use as remedies for aches and fever. The Greek physician Hippocrates documented their medicinal benefits in the 5th century BCE. Native Americans across the American continent also relied on willow as a staple in their medical treatments. In 1763, Reverend Edward Stone in England observed the medicinal properties of willow bark and reported his findings to the Royal Society. The active extract, salicin, was isolated in crystalline form in 1828 by French pharmacist Henri Leroux and Italian chemist Raffaele Piria, who further purified it into salicylic acid. In 1897, Felix Hoffmann synthesized a modified version of salicin (derived from the Spiraea plant) that caused less digestive upset than pure salicylic acid. This new drug, acetylsalicylic acid, was named aspirin by Hoffmann's employer, Bayer AG. Aspirin became the foundation for the development of the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) class, which remains critically important in modern medicine. Other Uses Willows are one of the four species used during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot. Living willow sculptures are created using the flexible branches of the tree. Willow in Human Culture Willows have been a prominent subject in the cultural traditions of many East Asian nations. In Korea, for example, willows are frequently mentioned in poetry. Gisaeng Hongrang, a poet from the mid-Joseon period, wrote a famous poem inspired by a willow tree in the rain during the evening, symbolizing her parting from a lover. The poem reflects the deep cultural and emotional significance of the willow tree.
